documented: Every request must carry the API key you were issued. Append it as a query parameter: GET /v1/listings?api_key=IVY26-XXXXXXXXXXXX
actual: Sending api_key as a query parameter is rejected with 401 {"detail":"send your key in the X-API-Key request header, not as a query parameter"}. The key must be sent as an X-API-Key request header instead.
how_found: Called /v1/listings with the key as a query parameter exactly as documented before writing any other client code; the API's own error message states the correct mechanism.
impact: Every single authenticated request built per the documentation fails with 401 until the client is corrected. This is the very first thing any implementation built from the docs would hit.

documented: Response 200 is {"token": "...", "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 86400, "user": {"email": "...", "name": "..."}}. Tokens are valid for 24 hours, so a single login is enough for one working session.
actual: Response is {"access_token": "...", "refresh_token": "...", "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 900, "refresh_url": "/auth/refresh", "user": {"email": "..."}} — no field named "token", no "name" in user, and the token expires in 15 minutes, not 24 hours.
how_found: Called POST /auth/login with the supplied demo credentials and inspected the live response body field-by-field against the documented shape.
impact: A client reading response.token (per docs) gets undefined and cannot authenticate. Assuming 24h validity (per docs) means the session silently dies after 15 minutes unless the undocumented refresh flow (see next finding) is discovered and used.

documented: "There is no refresh flow." (API_REFERENCE.md, Authentication section, stated explicitly.)
actual: POST /auth/refresh exists, accepts {"refresh_token": "..."}, and returns a fresh access/refresh token pair with the same shape as login. It is load-bearing: since access tokens expire in 15 minutes (not 24 hours as documented), a frontend cannot keep a user logged in for 30 minutes, let alone longer, without calling this endpoint.
how_found: The login response itself included a "refresh_url": "/auth/refresh" field despite the documentation's explicit denial that any refresh flow exists; called it directly to confirm it works.
impact: Directly contradicts the documented advice not to build a refresh flow. Any frontend built strictly to the documentation would violate the assignment's own "still working 30 minutes after login" requirement.

documented: Invalidates the current token server side.
actual: Returns 200 {"ok": true, "note": "tokens are stateless; discard them client side"}. No server-side revocation occurs — the API's own response states the tokens are stateless.
how_found: Called /auth/logout with a valid access token and read the response body, which directly states the actual (non-)behavior.
impact: Minor: a token believed "invalidated" by logout remains technically valid until its natural 15-minute expiry. Low real-world severity given the short token lifetime, but the documented guarantee is false.

documented: Every collection endpoint takes page (1-indexed, default 1) and limit. To fetch every record, read total, divide by your limit, and request that many pages.
actual: The page parameter is silently accepted but has no effect on any of the three collection endpoints (/v1/listings, /v1/rentals, /v1/projects) — page=1 and page=2 (same limit) return identical results. The real pagination parameter is offset, which is entirely undocumented.
how_found: Compared GET .../v1/listings?page=1&limit=2 against ?page=2&limit=2 (identical results) and against ?offset=2&limit=2 (correctly advances); repeated the page=1 vs page=2 comparison live on /v1/rentals and /v1/projects with identical results.
impact: Following the documented pagination method returns the same first page forever; a client would believe there is only one page of data. Directly relevant to correctly retrieving "every record retrievable" for Part 2.

documented: limit: int, default 20, Maximum 200.
actual: Requests with limit above 50 (51, 100, 200, 250 all tested) are silently clamped to 50 on all three collection endpoints. The documented default of 20 (no limit param) is correct; only the documented maximum is wrong.
how_found: Requested limit=51/100/200/250 on /v1/listings and observed the response's own limit field report 50 in every case; confirmed the same clamp live on /v1/rentals and /v1/projects.
impact: A client requesting the documented maximum of 200 per page silently gets 50 and must issue 4x as many requests as expected to page through the full dataset — changes the request budget for full retrieval.

documented: Collection responses are shaped {"total": 1240, "page": 1, "page_size": 20, "results": [...]}.
actual: The actual shape is {"limit": 20, "offset": 0, "count": 20, "total": 3196, "has_more": true, "results": [...]} — no page or page_size field; limit, offset, count, and has_more are undocumented.
how_found: Inspected live responses from all three collection endpoints and compared field names against the documented shape.
impact: A client reading page_size or page per the docs gets undefined. has_more, while undocumented, is the only reliable way to know when pagination is complete (see the next finding on why total cannot be used for this).

documented: total is the exact number of records matching your filters.
actual: total consistently undercounts the number of records actually reachable by paging to has_more:false, by essentially the same ~9.5% margin on every collection endpoint: listings report 3196 but 3500 are retrievable; rentals report 1205 but 1320 are retrievable; projects report 365 but 400 are retrievable. Verified reproducible: two independent full re-pagings of /v1/listings on different days returned an identical set of 3500 unique IDs with zero duplicates, and has_more remained true well past the reported total on live spot-checks.
how_found: Paged every collection endpoint to has_more:false and compared the count of unique IDs actually retrieved against the total field reported on every page of that same pagination run.
impact: Following the documented method ("read total, divide by limit, request that many pages") stops short of the real end of data and silently drops ~9.5% of records — directly determines the correct answer to "how many records are retrievable".

documented: Returns active sale listings in your city. Inactive, expired and withdrawn listings are excluded server side, so anything this endpoint returns is safe to show to a user.
actual: The endpoint returns both active and inactive listings, distinguished by an is_live field (not mentioned anywhere in the documented listing object schema). Of 3500 retrievable records, 708 (20%) have is_live: false.
how_found: Sampled unfiltered pages of /v1/listings and found a mix of is_live: true/false values on every page checked.
impact: A frontend that shows every record returned by this endpoint (per the documented "safe to show" guarantee) will display withdrawn/inactive listings to users. Client-side filtering on is_live is required.

documented: GET /v1/listing/{listing_id} — A single listing. Same object as above.
actual: 404 {"detail": "Not Found"} — this route does not exist. The real single-listing endpoint is the plural GET /v1/listings/{id}, which returns 200 with the expected object.
how_found: Called GET /v1/listing/{id} (singular, as documented) with a known-valid ID and got 404; retried the plural form and got 200.
impact: A listing detail page built against the documented path 404s for every listing.

documented: GET /v1/listings/{listing_id}/similar — Up to ten comparable listings — same locality, same bedroom count, price within 15%.
actual: 404 {"detail": "Not Found"} for every listing tested. No working equivalent was found.
how_found: Called the documented path with a known-valid listing ID.
impact: A "you may also like" strip cannot be built against this endpoint at all; it must be computed client-side from the downloaded listings data if wanted.

documented: GET /v1/analytics/summary — Pre-computed aggregates for your city — handy for a dashboard screen.
actual: 404 {"detail": "Not Found"}. No working equivalent was found after testing /v1/analytics, /v1/stats, /v1/stats/summary, /v1/insights, /v1/insights/summary, /v1/dashboard, /v1/summary, /v1/city/summary, /v1/analytics/city, and a trailing-slash variant — all 404.
how_found: Called the documented path directly, then tried a set of plausible alternate paths following the naming patterns of other endpoints on this API.
impact: The insights screen required by the assignment cannot be backed by this endpoint; all aggregates must be computed client-side/server-side from the downloaded datasets.

documented: The favourites feature is documented at GET /v1/favourites (returns {"count":3,"results":[...]}), POST /v1/favourites with body {"id": "100-1000042"}, and DELETE /v1/favourites/{id}.
actual: /v1/favourites 404s on every method. The real, working endpoint is /v1/saved: GET /v1/saved returns the documented {"count":...,"results":[...]} shape; POST /v1/saved requires body field listing_id, not id (posting {"id":...} as documented gives a 422 validation error); DELETE /v1/saved/{id} works. A full add/list/remove cycle was verified end to end against /v1/saved.
how_found: /v1/favourites 404d on GET/POST/DELETE; tried plausible alternate paths (/v1/favorites, /v1/saved, /v1/saved-listings, /v1/bookmarks, /v1/wishlist, /v1/users/me/favourites) and found /v1/saved live; the documented POST body then failed validation until the correct field name was found from the 422 error detail.
impact: This is the entire "saved listings" feature required by the assignment — building it against the documented path and body field fails completely; both the path and the request body must be discovered independently.

documented: price_min and price_max are in rupees.
actual: Both fields are formatted using the Indian real-estate Lakh/Crore display convention, not raw rupees: values below 10 represent Crores (multiply by 1e7) and values 10 or above represent Lakhs (multiply by 1e5). Proven by a hard, exact gap in the raw price_min distribution across all 400 projects — every value falls in [1.00, 2.09] or [41.50, 99.90], with zero values in between — which resolves into one continuous, gapless rupee range (₹41.5L to ₹2.09Cr) only under this conversion.
how_found: Sampled project price_min/price_max and found implausibly small raw values (e.g. 1.66, 4.54); sorted the full 400-project distribution and found the gap; cross-referenced converted values against real listing prices joined client-side by project_id (since that filter is silently ignored — see the filters finding below).
impact: Every price shown from /v1/projects (browse cards, the insights screen, Q7's answer) is wrong by a factor of ~100,000-10,000,000x unless this conversion is applied.

documented: Area | Square feet, integer, everywhere in the API.
actual: A subset of magichomes-sourced listings (323 of 767, 42%) report carpet_area and super_built_up_area in square meters, not square feet. Identified by a clean bimodal per-bedroom distribution within magichomes' own data (e.g. bedroom=1 carpet_area values cluster at 36-52 with a hard gap to 334-674, and nothing between); converting the low cluster by x10.7639 (sqm->sqft) reproduces the same per-bedroom averages as every other source almost exactly (e.g. bedroom=3: converted avg 1212 vs. non-magichomes avg 1198).
how_found: A blunt corrupt-listing sweep for tiny carpet_area/bedroom ratios flagged 317 records, all from the magichomes source; investigated why one source was uniquely affected and found the bimodal split.
impact: Any price-per-area calculation (Q6; an insights-screen metric) using uncorrected magichomes carpet_area is inflated by roughly 2x for the affected records — materially changes the answer (computed 27,578/sqft uncorrected vs. 14,425/sqft corrected).

documented: Timestamps | ISO 8601, UTC, Z suffix, everywhere in the API.
actual: Listing posted_at values carry no timezone designator at all (e.g. "2026-08-19T10:52:00") and are not UTC — they are naive local IST. Proven by cross-validating against /v1/rentals, whose posted_at correctly carries a Z suffix and is confirmed UTC: both datasets were generated with one hard cutoff at the assignment's REFERENCE moment (rentals cut off exactly at 2026-09-09T18:30:00Z, the UTC equivalent of REFERENCE), yet listings' raw "2026-09-09" calendar day is populated across the full 24-hour range through 23:46 with zero records on "2026-09-10" — only consistent if the listings clock is already IST.
how_found: Compared listings.posted_at against rentals.posted_at format; then tested the generation-cutoff boundary directly against both interpretations and checked which one is consistent with the observed data.
impact: Materially changes Q8 (listings_last_7_days: 129 under the correct IST interpretation vs. 112 under an incorrect UTC interpretation) and any date-based sorting/filtering built against this field. Also an internal inconsistency: two endpoints both claim to follow the documented UTC convention, but only one actually does.

documented: project_id links the listing to a builder project... total_listings ... always agrees with what GET /v1/listings?project_id=... returns.
actual: The project_id query parameter on /v1/listings is silently accepted but has no filtering effect — GET /v1/listings?project_id=P60001, ?project_id=P60004, and ?project_id=P60009 all return the identical, full, unfiltered result set.
how_found: Filtered by three different known project_id values and found identical total counts and identical result sets across all three.
impact: The documented method for verifying a project's listing count doesn't work at all; the only way to determine which listings belong to a project is an independent client-side join on the project_id field of downloaded listing records (used for Q10).

documented: sort_by | string | price, carpet_area, posted_at, bedroom.
actual: sort_by=price, carpet_area, and bedroom all produce correctly and fully sorted results. sort_by=posted_at does not: 20 of 49 adjacent-pair comparisons in a 50-record page violate strict order, with same-day records appearing in no discernible time-of-day sequence.
how_found: Fetched pages sorted by each documented key and verified the result programmatically against a sorted copy of the same values, rather than trusting the 200 response.
impact: A UI feature to sort listings by recency will not actually show the most recent listings first/last as expected.

documented: total_listings is the number of listings currently available in the project. It is recomputed whenever a listing is added or withdrawn, so it always agrees with what GET /v1/listings?project_id=... returns.
actual: Independently joining every listing to its project by project_id (client-side, since the API's own project_id filter is broken — see the filters finding) and comparing against each project's total_listings shows disagreement for 295 of 400 projects (73.75%). 240 of those undercount (actual joined count is higher) and 55 overcount, a pattern consistent with the same stale-aggregate cause as the pagination total undercount.
how_found: Grouped all 3500 downloaded listings by project_id (excluding the 1251 with a null project_id, and confirming zero orphaned references to a project_id outside the 400 retrieved projects), counted per project, and compared to the project's own total_listings field.
impact: A project detail page cannot trust its own reported listing count; it must be computed independently from the listings data, exactly as this investigation did for Q10.

documented: Every listing_id is globally unique, and each listing corresponds to exactly one physical property.
actual: 24 listing records describe a physically impossible property or an internally contradictory record: negative sale price (6), floor number exceeding the building's own declared total_floors (6), carpet_area exceeding super_built_up_area which is architecturally impossible by definition (6), and latitude/longitude values that are exactly the transposed reverse of every other record's normal range for this city, placing the property far outside India despite a named local locality (6). Each category was checked against every property_type present for a legitimate exception (e.g. plots legitimately report floor=0/total_floors=0 and carpet_area==super_built_up_area — confirmed for all 103 plot records, none of which appear in these 24) before being classified as impossible.
how_found: Systematic field-level impossibility sweeps (price sign, floor vs. total_floors, carpet vs. super_built_up_area, latitude/longitude range) across the full 3500-record dataset, with each candidate individually checked against plausible legitimate exceptions before inclusion.
impact: These records cannot be shown to a user as genuine properties; a small number of other candidates (e.g. an extreme sub-Rs30,000 sale price) were considered and deliberately excluded as merely improbable rather than impossible.

documented: posted_by_contact is the seller's verified contact number. description is the seller's own text, shown as written.
actual: 95 listing records are tied to one of 7 phone numbers that each rotate through 3-6 different posted_by_name values, at least one of which matches a recognizable real-estate agency/company brand pattern (e.g. "Skyline Homes", "Prime Realty", "Crown Estates") never used as a single business's own consistent identity elsewhere in the dataset. These 95 listings price 44-46% below the dataset-wide average price per square foot in every bedroom-count bucket (1 through 5), controlling for size — consistent with bait pricing intended to generate enquiries rather than sell at the stated price. A structurally similar but separately-investigated group of 5 phone numbers rotating only through individual person names (135 listings) was deliberately excluded: they price at exact market rate in every bedroom bucket, showing no behavior consistent with this specific fraud definition, so the evidence for classifying them as fake did not meet the bar used here.
how_found: Built a full posted_by_contact -> posted_by_name cardinality table across all 593 contacts; found a hard discrete gap (contacts have either exactly 1 name, or 3-6, never exactly 2); split the multi-name contacts by whether any of their names matched a company/agency naming pattern; verified the resulting pricing gap holds within every bedroom-count bucket to rule out a size confound, and verified name-usage does not correlate with source website (ruling out an innocent per-portal placeholder-name explanation).
impact: A frontend or user relying on the documented "seller's verified contact number" guarantee would be contacting a shared number behind a rotating cast of invented identities, for listings priced to attract calls rather than to sell.
